Corollary E.25 (Conditions for Exact Equivalence).

The meta-score equals the integrated SDE score error exactly when:

  1. 1.

    N→∞N\to\infty (infinite data limit),

  2. 2.

    The model class contains the true conditional 𝔼⁡[y|𝐱]\mathbb{E}[y|\mathbf{x}] (realizability),

  3. 3.

    The boosting algorithm has converged: DKL(p0∗∥pm,0)<ϵD_{\text{KL}}(p_{0}^{*}\|p_{m,0})<\epsilon for arbitrarily small ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

In practice, the approximation quality is controlled by the sample size NN and the residual variance at step mm.

E.4 Global Optimality of the Greedy Trajectory

We have proven that each step of the gradient boosting algorithm is locally optimal, guided by a meta-score that seeks to correct the integrated error of the underlying SDE’s dynamics. However, this local optimality does not, in itself, guarantee that the sequence of greedy choices made by the algorithm constitutes a globally optimal path through the space of SDEs. A myopic, locally optimal decision can sometimes lead to a suboptimal overall trajectory.

To prove global optimality, we will now formalize the entire boosting process as a sequential decision problem. We will first define a single, global objective function that represents the total error over the entire trajectory. We will then use the calculus of dynamic programming, specifically the Bellman principle of optimality, to prove that the greedy, stage-wise algorithm is not a heuristic, but is in fact the provably optimal solution to this global problem.

E.4.1 The Global Trajectory Score Matching (GTSM) Objective

To analyze global optimality, we must first define the ideal problem we are trying to solve. The total error of our constructed trajectory is the sum of the local errors at each step of refinement.

Definition E.26 (Discrete Global Trajectory Score Matching (DGTSM) Objective).

The Discrete Global Trajectory Score Matching (DGTSM) objective is the sum of the individual Denoising Score Matching losses over the entire boosting trajectory:

ℒGTSM=∑m=0M−1𝔼(𝐱,y)∼p0⋆​[‖hm+1​(𝐱)−∇Fm​log​p​(y|Fm​(𝐱))‖2],\mathcal{L}_{\text{GTSM}}=\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},y)\sim p_{0}^{\star}}\left[\left\|h_{m+1}(\mathbf{x})-\nabla_{F_{m}}\log p(y|F_{m}(\mathbf{x}))\right\|^{2}\right], (68)

where the weak learner hm+1h_{m+1} is the chosen refinement operator at step mm. This objective measures the total squared error in following the optimal meta-score at every stage of the trajectory construction.

From Theorem E.22, we know that for the squared error loss, the optimal meta-score is proportional to the residual. The DGTSM objective is therefore equivalent to minimizing the sum of the squared errors of the weak learners with respect to the residuals at each step. This is precisely the objective that the stage-wise boosting algorithm seeks to minimize.

E.4.2 Provable Optimality via the Bellman Principle

Having established a global objective, we must now prove that the specific algorithm used—greedy, stage-wise optimization—is the optimal procedure for solving it. To do this with full rigor, we now reformulate the problem in the formal language of dynamic programming and sequential decision-making.

We first begin with a quick lemma, before moving onto our core formulation.

Lemma E.27 (Finite ϵ\epsilon-Net for Weak Learners).

For any bounded subset ℋbounded⊂𝒜\mathcal{H}_{\text{bounded}}\subset\mathcal{A} of weak learners with suph∈ℋbounded‖h‖∞≤B\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{bounded}}}\|h\|_{\infty}\leq B and VC dimension VV, and for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists a finite subset 𝒜ϵ⊂ℋbounded\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}\subset\mathcal{H}_{\text{bounded}} such that:

suph∈ℋboundedminh′∈𝒜ϵ⁡𝔼⁡[‖h⁡(𝐱)−h′​(𝐱)‖2]<ϵ,\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{bounded}}}\min_{h^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}}\mathbb{E}[\|h(\mathbf{x})-h^{\prime}(\mathbf{x})\|^{2}]<\epsilon, (69)

and |𝒜ϵ|≤(C​B/ϵ)O⁡(V)|\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon}|\leq(CB/\epsilon)^{O(V)} for some constant CC.

Proof.

This follows from standard covering number bounds for function classes with finite VC dimension (see Theorem 2.6.7 in van der Vaart and Wellner (1996)). Decision trees with depth dd have VC dimension O⁡(d⋅log⁡d)O(d\cdot\log d), yielding polynomial-sized ϵ\epsilon-nets. ∎

Next, we define the boosting process as a sequential task allowing us to invoke Dynamic Programming.

Definition E.28 (The Boosting Process as a Sequential Decision Problem).

The optimization of the DGTSM objective is a finite-horizon, deterministic sequential decision problem defined by the tuple (𝒮,𝒜,T,C)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},T,C):

  • •

    Time Steps: The discrete boosting iterations m∈{0,1,…,M}m\in\{0,1,\dots,M\}.

  • •

    State Space 𝒮\mathcal{S}: The space of all SDEs representable by canonical net decision trees. The state at step mm is Sm∈𝒮S_{m}\in\mathcal{S}.

  • •

    Action Space 𝒜\mathcal{A}: The space of all possible weak learners. The action at step mm is hm+1∈𝒜h_{m+1}\in\mathcal{A}.

  • •

    Transition Function TT: A deterministic function T:𝒮×𝒜→𝒮T:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{S}, where the next state Sm+1=T⁡(Sm,hm+1)S_{m+1}=T(S_{m},h_{m+1}) is uniquely defined by the partition refinement and the mapping from Section E.1.4.

  • •

    Stage Cost CC: A function C:𝒮×𝒜→ℝC:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}, where the cost of taking action hm+1h_{m+1} from state SmS_{m} is the DSM loss: C⁡(Sm,hm+1)=𝔼⁡[‖hm+1−rm+1‖2]C(S_{m},h_{m+1})=\mathbb{E}[\|h_{m+1}-r_{m+1}\|^{2}].

  • •

    Policy π\pi: A sequence of decision functions, π=(π0,…,πM−1)\pi=(\pi_{0},\dots,\pi_{M-1}), where πm​(Sm)=hm+1\pi_{m}(S_{m})=h_{m+1} is the action to take in state SmS_{m}.

  • •

    Total Cost J⁡(π)J(\pi): The DGTSM objective for a given policy: J⁡(π)=∑m=0M−1C⁡(Sm,πm​(Sm))J(\pi)=\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}C(S_{m},\pi_{m}(S_{m})).

The optimization problem is to find an optimal policy π⋆\pi^{\star} that minimizes the total cost, J⁡(π)J(\pi). By Lemma E.27, for each step mm and precision ϵm>0\epsilon_{m}>0, we can restrict attention to a finite action space 𝒜ϵm\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon_{m}} that ϵm\epsilon_{m}-approximates the full action space. We analyze optimality over this finite discretization, then take ϵm→0\epsilon_{m}\to 0.

To solve this, we use the foundational principle of dynamic programming.

Theorem E.29 (Bellman’s Principle of Optimality).

An optimal policy has the property that whatever the initial state and initial decision are, the remaining decisions must constitute an optimal policy with regard to the state resulting from the first decision (Bertsekas, 2012).

Theorem E.30 (Optimality of the Greedy Trajectory).

The greedy policy, πG\pi^{G}, which at each step mm chooses the weak learner hm+1h_{m+1} that minimizes the immediate stage cost C⁡(Sm,hm+1)C(S_{m},h_{m+1}), is the globally optimal policy for the DGTSM problem.

Proof.

We prove this by backward induction. Let Vm​(Sm)V_{m}(S_{m}) be the optimal cost-to-go from state SmS_{m} at step mm to the end of the process (i.e., the minimum possible sum of costs from step mm to M−1M-1).

By Lemma E.27, for each step mm and precision ϵm>0\epsilon_{m}>0, we can restrict attention to a finite action space 𝒜ϵm\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon_{m}} that ϵm\epsilon_{m}-approximates the full action space. We analyze optimality over this finite discretization, then take ϵm→0\epsilon_{m}\to 0.

  1. 1.

    Base Case (m=M−1m=M-1): At the final stage, the decision is to choose hMh_{M} to transition from state SM−1S_{M-1}. The optimal cost-to-go is simply the minimum possible cost at this stage, as there are no future costs:

    VM−1​(SM−1)=minhM∈𝒜ϵM−1⁡C⁡(SM−1,hM).V_{M-1}(S_{M-1})=\min_{h_{M}\in\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon_{M-1}}}C(S_{M-1},h_{M}).

    The optimal action, πM−1⋆​(SM−1)\pi_{M-1}^{\star}(S_{M-1}), is by definition the greedy choice that minimizes this immediate cost.

  2. 2.

    Inductive Hypothesis: Assume that for all steps k>mk>m, the optimal policy πk⋆\pi_{k}^{\star} is the greedy policy.

  3. 3.

    Inductive Step (mm): The Bellman equation for the optimal cost-to-go at step mm is:

    Vm​(Sm)=minhm+1∈𝒜⁡[C⁡(Sm,hm+1)+Vm+1​(T⁡(Sm,hm+1))].V_{m}(S_{m})=\min_{h_{m+1}\in\mathcal{A}}\left[C(S_{m},h_{m+1})+V_{m+1}(T(S_{m},h_{m+1}))\right].

    Over the finite action space 𝒜ϵm\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon_{m}}, the minimum in the Bellman equation is well-defined:

    Vm​(Sm)=minhm+1∈𝒜ϵm⁡[C⁡(Sm,hm+1)+Vm+1​(T⁡(Sm,hm+1))].V_{m}(S_{m})=\min_{h_{m+1}\in\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon_{m}}}\left[C(S_{m},h_{m+1})+V_{m+1}(T(S_{m},h_{m+1}))\right].

    The crucial insight is that the problem structure is additively separable. The total cost is a simple sum of stage costs. The term Vm+1​(T⁡(Sm,hm+1))V_{m+1}(T(S_{m},h_{m+1})) represents the optimal future cost starting from the next state, Sm+1S_{m+1}. By our inductive hypothesis, the policy for all future steps is greedy and fixed. Therefore, the value Vm+1​(Sm+1)V_{m+1}(S_{m+1}) depends only on the state Sm+1S_{m+1} and not on how we choose to act at step mm or any future step.

    Because the stage cost C⁡(Sm,hm+1)C(S_{m},h_{m+1}) depends only on the current state SmS_{m} (which defines the residuals) and the current action hm+1h_{m+1}, the minimization decouples. The greedy choice over 𝒜ϵm\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon_{m}} is:

    hm+1ϵm=arg⁡minh∈𝒜ϵm⁡C⁡(Sm,h).h_{m+1}^{\epsilon_{m}}=\arg\min_{h\in\mathcal{A}_{\epsilon_{m}}}C(S_{m},h).

    As ϵm→0\epsilon_{m}\to 0, the discretization error vanishes. In the limit, the optimal policy converges to the greedy policy over the full action space:

    πm∗(Sm)=limϵm→0hm+1ϵm=arginfh∈𝒜C(Sm,h).\pi_{m}^{*}(S_{m})=\lim_{\epsilon_{m}\to 0}h_{m+1}^{\epsilon_{m}}=\arg\inf_{h\in\mathcal{A}}C(S_{m},h).

    Therefore, the optimal action πm⋆​(Sm)\pi_{m}^{\star}(S_{m}) is the greedy action.

By the principle of backward induction, the greedy policy is globally optimal for all steps. The gradient boosting algorithm, which at every stage fits a weak learner to the residuals, is a direct implementation of this optimal greedy policy. ∎

Corollary E.31 (The Optimal Policy is the SDE).

The optimal policy π⋆=(π0⋆,…,πM−1⋆)\pi^{\star}=(\pi_{0}^{\star},\dots,\pi_{M-1}^{\star}) is the sequence of optimal weak learners {h1⋆,…,hM⋆}\{h_{1}^{\star},\dots,h_{M}^{\star}\}. This sequence, by construction, uniquely defines the final, optimal net decision tree 𝒯M\mathcal{T}_{M} and its corresponding canonical model, SDEM\text{SDE}_{M}. Therefore, the optimal policy is the optimal SDE.

This completes the proof. We have shown that the simple, local, and greedy update rule of gradient boosting is not a heuristic, but a principled and provably optimal algorithm for solving a global score-matching problem over an entire coarse-to-fine trajectory in the space of continuous-time models.

Appendix F Implications of the GTSM Framework: A Unifying View of Score-Based Objectives

We further explore the deeper theoretical implications of our framework, showing that a single, global objective underpins a wide variety of modern score-based training methods. It is well-known in the theory of stochastic processes that matching the marginal distributions of two processes is a weaker condition than matching their full path-space measures (Lai et al., 2025). The latter is the strongest possible notion of equivalence but is generally intractable.

In this section, we first define a Continuous Global Trajectory Score Matching (CGTSM) objective for a general score-based model and prove, using Girsanov’s theorem (Oksendal, 2013), that it is equivalent to full path matching. We then demonstrate that several distinct and popular training objectives, including the simple diffusion loss, weighted diffusion losses, and consistency models can be rigorously derived as principled approximations or special cases of this single, master objective. This reveals that the boosting framework we analyze is not an isolated case but rather one instance of a broader class of algorithms that tractably solve this fundamental trajectory-matching problem. While the boosting DGTSM sums local errors over discrete refinement steps, the general CGTSM integrates score matching error over the continuous time horizon of an SDE. The boosting construction can thus be viewed as a discrete approximation of this continuous objective.

F.1 The Continuous GTSM Objective and Its Equivalence to Path Matching

Definition F.1 (The Continuous GTSM Objective).

Let S∗S^{*} be the ideal SDE with law ℙ∗\mathbb{P}^{*} and score functions 𝐬t∗​(𝐱)\mathbf{s}_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{x}). Let 𝐬θ​(𝐱,t)\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},t) be a parameterized score-based model. The Global Trajectory Score Matching (GTSM) objective is the integrated Fisher Divergence between the model’s score and the true score over the entire time horizon of the process:

ℒCGTSM​(θ)=12​∫0Tw⁡(t)⋅𝔼pt∗​(𝐱)​[‖𝐬θ​(𝐱,t)−𝐬t∗​(𝐱)‖𝐃⁡(t)2]​𝑑t,\mathcal{L}_{\text{CGTSM}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}w(t)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{x})}\left[\left\|\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},t)-\mathbf{s}_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{x})\right\|^{2}_{\mathbf{D}(t)}\right]dt, (70)

where w⁡(t)>0w(t)>0 is a weighting function and ‖𝐯‖𝐃2=𝐯⊤​𝐃𝐯\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{D}}=\mathbf{v}^{\top}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{v} is the Mahalanobis norm induced by the diffusion tensor 𝐃⁡(t)\mathbf{D}(t).

This objective is deeply connected to the KL divergence between path-space measures.

Proposition F.2 (Girsanov’s Theorem for SDEs).

Let ℙ∗\mathbb{P}^{*} be the law on path space induced by an Itô process with drift 𝐛∗\mathbf{b}^{*} and diffusion σ\sigma. Let ℙθ\mathbb{P}_{\theta} be the law induced by a second process with a different drift, 𝐛θ\mathbf{b}_{\theta}. If the Novikov condition is satisfied, the KL divergence between the two path-space measures is given by:

DKL(ℙ∗||ℙθ)=12𝔼ℙ∗[∫0T‖σ−1(𝐛∗−𝐛θ)‖2dt].D_{\text{KL}}(\mathbb{P}^{*}||\mathbb{P}_{\theta})=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}^{*}}\left[\int_{0}^{T}\left\|\sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{b}^{*}-\mathbf{b}_{\theta})\right\|^{2}dt\right]. (71)
Corollary F.3 (CGTSM Optimality Implies Path Matching).

A score model 𝐬θ\mathbf{s}_{\theta} achieves zero loss under the CGTSM objective with any strictly positive weighting w⁡(t)>0w(t)>0 if and only if the path-space measure ℙθ\mathbb{P}_{\theta} it induces is identical to the ideal path-space measure ℙ∗\mathbb{P}^{*}.

Proof.

The reverse drift of a diffusion process is a function of its score: 𝐛rev​(𝐱,t)=[−𝐛⁡(𝐱,t)+𝐃⁡(𝐱,t)​𝐬t​(𝐱)]\mathbf{b}_{\text{rev}}(\mathbf{x},t)=[-\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x},t)+\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{x},t)\mathbf{s}_{t}(\mathbf{x})]. Therefore, the difference in the drifts of two reverse-time processes is directly proportional to the difference in their score functions. Substituting this into the Girsanov formula for the KL divergence between the reverse-time path measures shows that DKL(ℙrev∗||ℙrev,θ)D_{\text{KL}}(\mathbb{P}_{\text{rev}}^{*}||\mathbb{P}_{\text{rev},\theta}) is an integral of the squared score error. The GTSM objective is a positively weighted integral of this same quantity. The objective is zero if and only if the integrand—the score error—is zero for almost all tt. By Girsanov’s theorem, this implies the KL divergence is zero, which holds if and only if the path measures are identical. ∎

Remark F.4 (On the Suitability of the Novikov Condition).

The validity of Girsanov’s theorem hinges on the Novikov condition, which is a regularity assumption that is met by both sides of our proposed equivalence, albeit for different reasons.

For the continuous flow side (standard score-based models), the condition is typically satisfied. The drift difference, Δ​𝐛rev=𝐃⁡(𝐬t∗−𝐬θ)\Delta\mathbf{b}_{\text{rev}}=\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{s}_{t}^{*}-\mathbf{s}_{\theta}), is well-behaved because the process operates on a finite-dimensional Gaussian measure, the score model 𝐬θ\mathbf{s}_{\theta} is a Lipschitz-continuous neural network, and the integration is over a finite time horizon. The theoretical challenges associated with infinite-dimensional function spaces, which would require the Wiener measure and different analytical tools such as those used for neural operators, are outside the scope of this standard setup.

For the discrete tree side, satisfaction of the condition is a direct and non-trivial consequence of our Tree-to-Flow mapping. A naive interpretation of a tree’s splits as instantaneous jumps would indeed violate the condition. However, our dyadic refinement procedure is precisely the mechanism that guarantees a continuous-path limit for the induced probability flow. This ensures the resulting drift is well-behaved and the Novikov condition holds. The condition would fail for processes characterized by irreducible, finite jumps that cannot be smoothed away—analogous to models of punctuated equilibria. Such processes would require a different mathematical formalism based on Lévy processes and are beyond the scope of our current framework.

Thus, the Novikov condition is a mild and well-justified regularity assumption within our framework, holding for standard diffusion models by construction and for tree-derived flows via our refinement theorem.

F.2 Deriving Standard Training Objectives as Special Cases of the CGTSM

The CGTSM objective is the ideal, but practical algorithms must approximate it. We now demonstrate that several popular training objectives are not ad-hoc heuristics, but can be rigorously derived as principled approximations of the CGTSM, each embodying a different inductive bias about the learning trajectory. The CGTSM framework’s true utility is that it provides a language for describing and justifying these biases. The objective is an integral over the filtration of tail-equivalence classes {𝒦t}\{\mathcal{K}_{t}\}, and each practical objective makes a different choice about how to prioritize or approximate the score matching loss for these classes.

The Simple Diffusion Loss.

The most common training objective is the simple, unweighted loss (Ho et al., 2020).

Proposition F.5.

The simple diffusion loss, ℒsimple=𝔼t∼U⁡(0,T),𝐱0,ϵ​[‖𝐬θ​(𝐱t,t)−∇𝐱t​log​pt​(𝐱t|𝐱0)‖2]\mathcal{L}_{\text{simple}}=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim U(0,T),\mathbf{x}_{0},\epsilon}[\|\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)-\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\mathbf{x}_{0})\|^{2}], is the unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of the unweighted CGTSM objective, where w⁡(t)=1w(t)=1. This corresponds to an inductive bias of uniform importance across all tail-equivalence classes.

Proof.

Setting w⁡(t)=1w(t)=1 in the CGTSM objective gives 12​∫0T𝔼pt∗​[‖𝐬θ−𝐬t∗‖𝐃2]​𝑑t\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}^{*}}[\|\mathbf{s}_{\theta}-\mathbf{s}_{t}^{*}\|^{2}_{\mathbf{D}}]dt. Using the equivalence of denoising score matching, the intractable true score 𝐬t∗\mathbf{s}_{t}^{*} can be replaced by the tractable conditional score ∇𝐱t​log​pt​(𝐱t|𝐱0)\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\mathbf{x}_{0}). The objective becomes an expectation over a uniform distribution in time, 𝔼t∼U⁡(0,T)​[…]\mathbb{E}_{t\sim U(0,T)}[\dots]. A single-sample Monte Carlo estimator for this integral is to sample a single time tt, a single data point 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}, and a single noise sample ϵ\epsilon, and compute the squared error. This is precisely the simple diffusion loss objective. This choice implicitly assumes that the learning difficulty is uniform across all time, or that a simple, unbiased estimate is sufficient. ∎

The Weighted Diffusion Loss.

Many state-of-the-art models use a non-uniform weighting λ⁡(t)\lambda(t) in their loss function (Kingma et al., 2021; Karras et al., 2024). The CGTSM framework reveals this as an explicit injection of bias.

Proposition F.6.

The weighted diffusion loss, ℒweighted=𝔼t,𝐱0,ϵ​[λ⁡(t)⋅‖𝐬θ​(𝐱t,t)−∇𝐱t​log​pt​(𝐱t|𝐱0)‖2]\mathcal{L}_{\text{weighted}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,\mathbf{x}_{0},\epsilon}[\lambda(t)\cdot\|\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)-\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}|\mathbf{x}_{0})\|^{2}], is an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of the CGTSM objective with a weighting function w⁡(t)=λ⁡(t)w(t)=\lambda(t). This choice injects a quantifiable bias, prioritizing the matching of score functions for specific tail-equivalence classes.

Proof.

The proof follows identically to the simple case. The weighting function λ⁡(t)\lambda(t) inside the expectation is the Monte Carlo estimator for the weighted integral where the CGTSM weight is w⁡(t)=λ⁡(t)w(t)=\lambda(t). This choice is motivated by (Assumption E.14). If a learner is intrinsically biased to learn the coarse tail-equivalence classes (large tt) first, an engineer can inject a counter-balancing bias by choosing a weighting function λ⁡(t)\lambda(t) that is larger for small tt. This forces the optimizer to pay more attention to the harder-to-learn, fine-grained details, thereby balancing the learning process across the entire trajectory. ∎

Consistency Models.

Consistency models are a state of the art framework that enforce self-consistency along the probability flow ODE trajectories (Song et al., 2023). We now show this injects a structural bias between tail-equivalence classes.

Proposition F.7.

The consistency distillation loss is an approximation of the CGTSM objective that injects a strong inductive bias on the coupling between adjacent tail-equivalence classes.

Proof.

The consistency loss is of the form ℒconsist=𝔼⁡[d⁡(fθ​(𝐱t2,t2),fθ′​(𝐱t1,t1))]\mathcal{L}_{\text{consist}}=\mathbb{E}[d(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t_{2}},t_{2}),f_{\theta^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x}_{t_{1}},t_{1}))], where fθf_{\theta} is the student, fθ′f_{\theta^{\prime}} is a teacher model, and 𝐱t1,𝐱t2\mathbf{x}_{t_{1}},\mathbf{x}_{t_{2}} are adjacent points on an ODE trajectory. Standard DSM-based objectives learn the score for each time tt (and thus for each class 𝒦t\mathcal{K}_{t}) independently. The consistency loss, in contrast, imposes a strong structural constraint: the model’s behavior for class 𝒦t2\mathcal{K}_{t_{2}} must be directly predictable from its behavior for class 𝒦t1\mathcal{K}_{t_{1}}. This enforces a smoothness condition along the trajectory of models. This bias is what enables rapid sampling: by learning the relationship between different points on the trajectory, the model can make larger, more informed jumps during inference. The consistency loss is therefore a specific, bootstrapped approximation of the GTSM objective that prioritizes trajectory smoothness over pointwise score accuracy. ∎

This unified perspective reveals that these different training objectives are not ad-hoc heuristics but are deeply connected, principled variations of a single, fundamental goal: matching the entire generative trajectory. The gradient boosting algorithm, as we have shown, is a provably optimal, constructive solver for this same master objective.

Appendix G DSM-Tree: Discretized Score Matching for Decision Trees

Having established the CGTSM framework as a unifying objective for trajectory-based learning, we now demonstrate its first concrete algorithmic instantiation: Discretized Score Matching for Trees (DSM-Tree). This algorithm addresses a fundamental problem in machine learning: how to distill the knowledge of a decision tree—a discrete, interpretable model—into a neural network that preserves the tree’s decision boundaries while gaining the benefits of continuous, differentiable representations.

The key insight is that a decision tree defines a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of decision boundaries, and learning this hierarchy is equivalent to performing score matching over the discrete trajectory defined by tree depth levels. DSM-Tree thus creates a neural network classifier whose learned decision function faithfully replicates the tree’s partition structure.

G.1 The Tree Distillation Problem

We define the tree distillation problem as the task of learning a neural network classifier fθ:𝒳→𝒴f_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} that approximates a trained decision tree 𝒯:𝒳→𝒴\mathcal{T}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} such that fθ​(𝐱)≈𝒯⁡(𝐱)∀𝐱∈𝒳,f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\approx\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})\quad\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}, while maintaining a continuous, differentiable representation that can generalize beyond the tree’s exact decision boundaries.

This problem presents two fundamental challenges. First, the tree’s Hierarchical Structure—a nested sequence of partitions—is lost when a network is trained only on the final outputs. Second, a naive distillation approach discards information about the unique Discrete Decision Paths each sample follows. DSM-Tree addresses both challenges by training a conditional network Mθ​(𝐱,j)M_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},j) that learns to predict the optimal decision at each tree level jj, explicitly modeling the hierarchical trajectory.

G.2 Algorithm Overview

DSM-Tree operates in three phases that mirror the theoretical structure developed in Appendices C and E:

The crucial innovation is that the neural network does not directly learn to map inputs to outputs. Instead, it learns the intermediate decision function at each level, thereby capturing the full hierarchical structure of the tree’s decision-making process.

The key insight is that Phase 2 directly implements the GTSM objective in the discrete setting, where the ”time” variable is the tree depth level jj.

G.3 Formal Problem Setup

Definition G.1 (Conditional Decision Problem).

Given a trained decision tree 𝒯\mathcal{T} with depth DD, for each sample 𝐱\mathbf{x} and tree level j∈{0,…,D−1}j\in\{0,\ldots,D-1\}, define the optimal decision function:

d∗​(𝐱,j)={0if ​𝐱​ should go left at level ​j1if ​𝐱​ should go right at level ​j⊥if ​𝐱​ has reached a leaf before level ​jd^{*}(\mathbf{x},j)=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }\mathbf{x}\text{ should go left at level }j\\ 1&\text{if }\mathbf{x}\text{ should go right at level }j\\ \bot&\text{if }\mathbf{x}\text{ has reached a leaf before level }j\end{cases} (72)

where the decision is determined by the unique path through 𝒯\mathcal{T} from root to the leaf containing 𝐱\mathbf{x}.

Definition G.2 (DSM-Tree Training Objective).

The DSM-Tree model Mθ:ℝd×{0,…,D−1}→Δ1M_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\{0,\ldots,D-1\}\to\Delta^{1} (where Δ1\Delta^{1} is the probability simplex over {0,1}\{0,1\}) is trained to minimize:

ℒDSM(θ)=𝔼(𝐱,y)∼pdata𝔼j∼Uniform​(0,D−1)[𝕀[d∗(𝐱,j)≠⊥]⋅ℓCE(Mθ(𝐱,j),d∗(𝐱,j))],\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},y)\sim p_{\text{data}}}\mathbb{E}_{j\sim\text{Uniform}(0,D-1)}\left[\mathbb{I}[d^{*}(\mathbf{x},j)\neq\bot]\cdot\ell_{\text{CE}}(M_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},j),d^{*}(\mathbf{x},j))\right], (73)

where ℓCE\ell_{\text{CE}} is the cross-entropy loss and 𝕀⁡[⋅]\mathbb{I}[\cdot] is the indicator function that masks out samples that have reached leaves.

G.4 Connection to CGTSM Framework

We now establish the formal connection between the DSM-Tree objective and the continuous CGTSM framework developed in Appendix F.

Theorem G.3 (DSM-Tree as Discrete CGTSM).

The DSM-Tree objective (73) is the discrete-time instantiation of the CGTSM objective with uniform weighting w⁡(t)=1w(t)=1 and time discretized to tree depth levels.

Proof.

We proceed by explicitly constructing the correspondence between the discrete tree hierarchy and the continuous-time SDE framework.

Step 1: Recall the CGTSM objective from Appendix F.

For a continuous-time process, CGTSM minimizes:

ℒCGTSM​(θ)=12​∫0Tw⁡(t)⋅𝔼pt∗​(𝐱)​[‖𝐬θ​(𝐱,t)−𝐬t∗​(𝐱)‖𝐃⁡(t)2]​𝑑t,\mathcal{L}_{\text{CGTSM}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}w(t)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{x})}\left[\left\|\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},t)-\mathbf{s}_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{x})\right\|^{2}_{\mathbf{D}(t)}\right]dt, (74)

where 𝐬t∗​(𝐱)=∇𝐱​log​pt∗​(𝐱)\mathbf{s}_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{x})=\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\log p_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{x}) is the true score function.

Step 2: Discretize time to tree depth levels.

By Theorem C.21, a decision tree of depth DD induces a discrete sequence of densities {p⁡(𝐱,k)}k=0D\{p(\mathbf{x},k)\}_{k=0}^{D} corresponding to the coarse-graining trajectory. We identify:

tj=jD⋅T,j∈{0,1,…,D},t_{j}=\frac{j}{D}\cdot T,\quad j\in\{0,1,\ldots,D\}, (75)

so that t0=0t_{0}=0 (leaves, fine-grained) and tD=Tt_{D}=T (root, maximum entropy).

The continuous-time integral becomes a Riemann sum:

ℒCGTSM​(θ)≈TD​∑j=0D−1w⁡(tj)⋅𝔼ptj∗​(𝐱)​[‖𝐬θ​(𝐱,tj)−𝐬tj∗​(𝐱)‖2].\mathcal{L}_{\text{CGTSM}}(\theta)\approx\frac{T}{D}\sum_{j=0}^{D-1}w(t_{j})\cdot\mathbb{E}_{p_{t_{j}}^{*}(\mathbf{x})}\left[\left\|\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},t_{j})-\mathbf{s}_{t_{j}}^{*}(\mathbf{x})\right\|^{2}\right]. (76)

Step 3: Relate score matching to decision prediction.

From Theorem E.24, the optimal direction of change for a sample at tree level jj is given by the score function. In the discrete tree setting, this ”direction” is encoded by the binary decision d∗​(𝐱,j)d^{*}(\mathbf{x},j).

More precisely, the score function 𝐬tj∗​(𝐱)\mathbf{s}_{t_{j}}^{*}(\mathbf{x}) points in the direction of increasing density. In the tree’s partition Πj\Pi_{j} at level jj, a sample 𝐱\mathbf{x} resides in some region Ri∈ΠjR_{i}\in\Pi_{j}. The optimal next step in the coarse-graining trajectory is to refine this region by splitting it into two sub-regions, RileftR_{i}^{\text{left}} and RirightR_{i}^{\text{right}}.

The decision d∗​(𝐱,j)d^{*}(\mathbf{x},j) encodes which sub-region 𝐱\mathbf{x} belongs to. This is the discrete analogue of the score’s directional information. The squared score error ‖𝐬θ−𝐬∗‖2\|\mathbf{s}_{\theta}-\mathbf{s}^{*}\|^{2} in the continuous case corresponds to the classification error in predicting d∗​(𝐱,j)d^{*}(\mathbf{x},j) in the discrete case.

Therefore, the score-matching term becomes:

‖𝐬θ(𝐱,tj)−𝐬tj∗(𝐱)‖2⟷ℓCE(Mθ(𝐱,j),d∗(𝐱,j)).\left\|\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},t_{j})-\mathbf{s}_{t_{j}}^{*}(\mathbf{x})\right\|^{2}\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad\ell_{\text{CE}}(M_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},j),d^{*}(\mathbf{x},j)). (77)

Step 4: Simplify for uniform weighting and data distribution.

Setting w⁡(t)=1w(t)=1 (uniform weighting) and taking expectations with respect to the empirical data distribution pdatap_{\text{data}}, the discrete CGTSM objective (76) becomes:

ℒCGTSMdiscrete​(θ)=∑j=0D−1𝔼𝐱∼pdata​[ℓCE​(Mθ​(𝐱,j),d∗​(𝐱,j))].\mathcal{L}_{\text{CGTSM}}^{\text{discrete}}(\theta)=\sum_{j=0}^{D-1}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim p_{\text{data}}}\left[\ell_{\text{CE}}(M_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},j),d^{*}(\mathbf{x},j))\right]. (78)

The indicator function 𝕀[d∗(𝐱,j)≠⊥]\mathbb{I}[d^{*}(\mathbf{x},j)\neq\bot] in (73) simply masks out samples that have reached leaves before level jj, which is necessary for well-defined training. The uniform distribution over jj in the expectation is the Monte Carlo sampling strategy for the sum over levels.

Therefore, ℒDSM​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}(\theta) is exactly the discrete-time, uniformly weighted CGTSM objective. ∎

G.5 Convergence Analysis

We now establish the finite-sample convergence guarantees for the DSM-Tree algorithm.

Assumption G.4 (Realizability and Regularity).
  1. 1.

    The model class ℳ={Mθ:θ∈Θ}\mathcal{M}=\{M_{\theta}:\theta\in\Theta\} contains a function that can represent the true decision function d∗​(𝐱,j)d^{*}(\mathbf{x},j) for all levels jj.

  2. 2.

    The base tree 𝒯\mathcal{T} has bounded depth D<∞D<\infty and bounded number of leaves L=O⁡(2D)L=O(2^{D}).

  3. 3.

    The feature space is bounded: ‖𝐱‖≤B\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq B for all 𝐱∈𝒳\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}.

  4. 4.

    The loss function ℓCE\ell_{\text{CE}} is GG-Lipschitz continuous in the model parameters.

Theorem G.5 (Finite-Sample Convergence of DSM-Tree).

Under Assumption G.4, let θ^T\hat{\theta}_{T} be the parameters obtained after TT gradient descent steps with learning rate η=O⁡(1/T)\eta=O(1/\sqrt{T}) and batch size BB. Then with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta:

ℒDSM​(θ^T)−ℒDSM​(θ∗)≤O⁡(D⋅d​log⁡(L/δ)B​T),\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}(\hat{\theta}_{T})-\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}(\theta^{*})\leq O\left(\frac{D\cdot\sqrt{d\log(L/\delta)}}{\sqrt{BT}}\right), (79)

where θ∗\theta^{*} is the optimal parameter and dd is the feature dimensionality.

Proof.

The proof follows the standard analysis of stochastic gradient descent for empirical risk minimization, adapted to the tree-structured setting.

We decompose the excess risk into optimization error and generalization error:

ℒDSM​(θ^T)−ℒDSM​(θ∗)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}(\hat{\theta}_{T})-\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}(\theta^{*}) =[ℒDSM​(θ^T)−ℒ^DSM​(θ^T)]⏟Generalization error\displaystyle=\underbrace{\left[\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}(\hat{\theta}_{T})-\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{DSM}}(\hat{\theta}_{T})\right]}_{\text{Generalization error}} (80)
+[ℒ^DSM​(θ^T)−ℒ^DSM​(θ∗)]⏟Optimization error\displaystyle\quad+\underbrace{\left[\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{DSM}}(\hat{\theta}_{T})-\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{DSM}}(\theta^{*})\right]}_{\text{Optimization error}} (81)
+[ℒ^DSM​(θ∗)−ℒDSM​(θ∗)]⏟Generalization error,\displaystyle\quad+\underbrace{\left[\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{DSM}}(\theta^{*})-\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}(\theta^{*})\right]}_{\text{Generalization error}}, (82)

where ℒ^DSM\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{DSM}} is the empirical loss on training data.

The DSM-Tree objective is a finite sum over tree levels jj. For each level jj, the per-sample loss ℓCE​(Mθ​(𝐱,j),d∗​(𝐱,j))\ell_{\text{CE}}(M_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},j),d^{*}(\mathbf{x},j)) is GG-Lipschitz and bounded by log⁡2\log 2 (for binary cross-entropy).

By standard SGD convergence for smooth, Lipschitz losses (Bottou et al., 2018), after TT steps with learning rate η=O⁡(1/T)\eta=O(1/\sqrt{T}):

ℒ^DSM​(θ^T)−ℒ^DSM​(θ∗)≤O⁡(G2T).\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{DSM}}(\hat{\theta}_{T})-\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{DSM}}(\theta^{*})\leq O\left(\frac{G^{2}}{\sqrt{T}}\right). (83)

We now, apply uniform convergence bounds for the hypothesis class ℳ\mathcal{M}. The key is to bound the complexity of the joint hypothesis class over both features 𝐱\mathbf{x} and levels jj.

Define the extended hypothesis class:

ℳ~={(𝐱,j)↦Mθ​(𝐱,j):θ∈Θ}.\tilde{\mathcal{M}}=\{(\mathbf{x},j)\mapsto M_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},j):\theta\in\Theta\}. (84)

The VC dimension of this class is bounded by:

VC​(ℳ~)≤VC​(ℳ)+log2⁡D,\text{VC}(\tilde{\mathcal{M}})\leq\text{VC}(\mathcal{M})+\log_{2}D, (85)

where the log2⁡D\log_{2}D term accounts for the discrete level variable.

For neural networks with WW parameters, VC​(ℳ)=O​(W​log⁡W)\text{VC}(\mathcal{M})=O(W\log W) (Bartlett, 1998). However, the tree structure provides additional structure: at each level jj, only O⁡(2j)O(2^{j}) nodes are active, so the effective VC dimension is:

VCeff​(j)=O⁡(W​log⁡W+j).\text{VC}_{\text{eff}}(j)=O\left(W\log W+j\right). (86)

Averaging over all levels j∈{0,…,D−1}j\in\{0,\ldots,D-1\}:

𝔼j​[VCeff​(j)]=O⁡(W​log⁡W+D).\mathbb{E}_{j}[\text{VC}_{\text{eff}}(j)]=O(W\log W+D). (87)

By the VC inequality (Vapnik, 1999), with NN training samples and batch size BB, the generalization error satisfies:

|ℒDSM​(θ)−ℒ^DSM​(θ)|≤O⁡(VCeff​log⁡(N/δ)B​T).\left|\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}(\theta)-\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{DSM}}(\theta)\right|\leq O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\text{VC}_{\text{eff}}\log(N/\delta)}{BT}}\right). (88)

The DSM-Tree objective sums over DD tree levels. Each level corresponds to a partition Πj\Pi_{j} with at most 2j2^{j} regions. The total number of decision boundaries across all levels is:

∑j=0D−12j=2D−1=L−1,\sum_{j=0}^{D-1}2^{j}=2^{D}-1=L-1, (89)

where LL is the number of leaves.

The effective sample complexity must account for learning all DD levels. By a union bound over levels, the generalization error becomes:

|ℒDSM​(θ)−ℒ^DSM​(θ)|≤O⁡(D⋅d​log⁡(L/δ)B​T),\left|\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}(\theta)-\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{DSM}}(\theta)\right|\leq O\left(\sqrt{\frac{D\cdot d\log(L/\delta)}{BT}}\right), (90)

where dd is the feature dimensionality (assuming the neural network has O⁡(d)O(d) parameters per level).

Combining the optimization and generalization error bounds:

ℒDSM​(θ^T)−ℒDSM​(θ∗)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}(\hat{\theta}_{T})-\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}(\theta^{*}) ≤O⁡(G2T)+O⁡(D⋅d​log⁡(L/δ)B​T)\displaystyle\leq O\left(\frac{G^{2}}{\sqrt{T}}\right)+O\left(\sqrt{\frac{D\cdot d\log(L/\delta)}{BT}}\right) (91)
=O⁡(D⋅d​log⁡(L/δ)B​T),\displaystyle=O\left(\frac{D\cdot\sqrt{d\log(L/\delta)}}{\sqrt{BT}}\right), (92)

where the second term dominates for large DD and the first term is absorbed using G=O⁡(D)G=O(D) (since the loss sums over levels).

This completes the proof. ∎

Remark G.6 (Dependence on Tree Depth).

The convergence rate’s dependence on tree depth DD is unavoidable: learning the entire coarse-to-fine trajectory requires resolving all DD levels of abstraction. However, the linear dependence on DD is optimal for this problem, as it matches the information-theoretic lower bound for learning a tree of depth DD.

Corollary G.7 (Path-Wise Consistency).

As T→∞T\to\infty and B​T/N→cBT/N\to c for some constant c>0c>0, the DSM-Tree model Mθ^TM_{\hat{\theta}_{T}} produces decision paths that converge to the ground-truth paths of the base tree 𝒯\mathcal{T} with probability 1:

limT→∞ℙ[PathMθ^T(𝐱)=Path𝒯(𝐱),∀𝐱∈𝒳]=1.\lim_{T\to\infty}\mathbb{P}\left[\text{Path}_{M_{\hat{\theta}_{T}}}(\mathbf{x})=\text{Path}_{\mathcal{T}}(\mathbf{x}),\,\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}\right]=1. (93)
Proof.

By Theorem G.5, ℒDSM​(θ^T)→ℒDSM​(θ∗)\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}(\hat{\theta}_{T})\to\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}(\theta^{*}) as T→∞T\to\infty. Since the loss is a sum of cross-entropy terms over all levels:

ℒDSM​(θ)=∑j=0D−1𝔼𝐱​[ℓCE​(Mθ​(𝐱,j),d∗​(𝐱,j))],\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}(\theta)=\sum_{j=0}^{D-1}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}}\left[\ell_{\text{CE}}(M_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},j),d^{*}(\mathbf{x},j))\right], (94)

and cross-entropy is zero if and only if Mθ​(𝐱,j)=d∗​(𝐱,j)M_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},j)=d^{*}(\mathbf{x},j) almost surely, we have:

ℒDSM​(θ)=0⇔Mθ​(𝐱,j)=d∗​(𝐱,j)​ for all ​𝐱,j.\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}(\theta)=0\iff M_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},j)=d^{*}(\mathbf{x},j)\text{ for all }\mathbf{x},j. (95)

Since θ∗\theta^{*} is the minimizer by Assumption G.4, this implies exact decision matching at every level. The path through the tree is determined by the sequence of decisions {dj}j=0D−1\{d_{j}\}_{j=0}^{D-1}, so exact decision matching implies exact path matching. ∎

G.6 Computational Complexity

Proposition G.8 (Training Complexity).

The computational complexity of training DSM-Tree for TT steps with batch size BB on a tree of depth DD is:

O⁡(T⋅B⋅D⋅Cnet),O(T\cdot B\cdot D\cdot C_{\text{net}}),

where CnetC_{\text{net}} is the cost of a forward-backward pass through the neural network MθM_{\theta}.

Proof.

Each training step’s complexity is dominated by several operations. For a batch of size BB, the algorithm must: (1) sample data points and tree levels (O⁡(B)O(B)); (2) traverse the teacher tree for each sample to find its ground-truth decision, which takes O⁡(D)O(D) time per sample, for a total of O⁡(B​D)O(BD); and (3) perform a forward and backward pass through the neural network, which costs O⁡(B⋅Cnet)O(B\cdot C_{\text{net}}). The network cost CnetC_{\text{net}} itself depends on the input size, which includes the feature dimension and the level embedding dimension. Since the tree traversal and network passes are the most expensive operations per batch, and this is repeated for TT training steps, the total complexity is driven by the sum of these costs, leading to the stated O⁡(T⋅B⋅D⋅Cnet)O(T\cdot B\cdot D\cdot C_{\text{net}}) complexity. ∎

Remark G.9 (Comparison to Standard Tree Training).

Standard decision tree training (e.g., CART) has complexity O⁡(N⋅d⋅D​log⁡D)O(N\cdot d\cdot D\log D), where NN is the number of samples. DSM-Tree’s complexity is O⁡(T⋅B⋅D⋅Cnet)O(T\cdot B\cdot D\cdot C_{\text{net}}). Since Cnet=O⁡(d⋅h)C_{\text{net}}=O(d\cdot h) for a network with hidden dimension hh, and typically T⋅B≈NT\cdot B\approx N (one epoch), the complexities are comparable when h=O⁡(log⁡D)h=O(\log D). However, DSM-Tree offers the advantage of learning a flexible, continuous representation of the tree structure.

Appendix H TreeFlow: Conditional Flow Matching with Tree-Structured Paths

We now present our second algorithmic instantiation: TreeFlow, which uses decision tree partitions to provide structured conditioning paths for conditional flow matching. Unlike DSM-Tree which creates neural classifiers by distilling tree boundaries, TreeFlow leverages tree-structured paths as ground truth trajectories for training generative flow models.

H.1 Algorithm Overview

TreeFlow combines conditional flow matching with tree-based partition encodings to create a partition-aware generative model.

Remark H.1 (TreeFlow and Conditional Flow Matching).

TreeFlow extends the Flow Matching framework (Lipman et al., 2023), which trains flow models via direct regression to conditional velocity fields along linear interpolation paths 𝐱(t)=t​𝐱data+(1−t)​𝐱noise\mathbf{x}^{(t)}=t\mathbf{x}^{\text{data}}+(1-t)\mathbf{x}^{\text{noise}}. The tree does not define these trajectories; rather, it provides conditioning information 𝐩\mathbf{p} that guides the velocity network vθ​(𝐱,t,𝐩,y)v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},t,\mathbf{p},y) to learn partition-specific flows, allowing the model to specialize to different regions of the data space based on its hierarchical organization.

H.2 Convergence Analysis for TreeFlow

We now establish finite-sample convergence guarantees for TreeFlow as a path-conditioned generative model.

Assumption H.2 (TreeFlow Regularity Conditions).
  1. 1.

    The data distribution pdata​(𝐱,y)p_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{x},y) has bounded support: ‖𝐱‖≤B\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq B for all 𝐱∈supp​(pdata)\mathbf{x}\in\text{supp}(p_{\text{data}}).

  2. 2.

    The base tree 𝒯\mathcal{T} has depth DD and L=O⁡(2D)L=O(2^{D}) leaves, with balanced partitioning (each leaf has comparable probability mass).

  3. 3.

    The velocity network vθv_{\theta} is GG-Lipschitz continuous in 𝐱\mathbf{x} and θ\theta.

  4. 4.

    The path encoding 𝐩=PathEncoder​(𝒯,𝐱)\mathbf{p}=\text{PathEncoder}(\mathcal{T},\mathbf{x}) is deterministic and has bounded norm: ‖𝐩‖≤P\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq P.

Theorem H.3 (Finite-Sample Convergence of TreeFlow).

Under Assumption H.2, let θ^S\hat{\theta}_{S} be the parameters obtained after SS gradient descent steps with learning rate η=O⁡(1/S)\eta=O(1/\sqrt{S}) and batch size BB. Then with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta:

ℒTreeFlow ​(θ^S)−ℒTreeFlow ​(θ∗)≤O⁡(d⋅L⋅log⁡(L/δ)B​S),\mathcal{L}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\hat{\theta}_{S})-\mathcal{L}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\theta^{*})\leq O\left(\frac{\sqrt{d\cdot L\cdot\log(L/\delta)}}{\sqrt{BS}}\right), (96)

where θ∗\theta^{*} is the optimal parameter and dd is the feature dimensionality.

Proof.

The proof follows a similar structure to the DSM-Tree convergence proof (Theorem G.5), with additional considerations for the continuous-time flow matching objective.

As before, we decompose:

ℒTreeFlow ​(θ^S)−ℒTreeFlow ​(θ∗)=(Generalization Error)+(Optimization Error).\mathcal{L}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\hat{\theta}_{S})-\mathcal{L}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\theta^{*})=\text{(Generalization Error)}+\text{(Optimization Error)}. (97)

The TreeFlow objective is:

ℒTreeFlow ​(θ)=𝔼t,𝐱(0),𝐱(1),𝐩,y​[‖vθ​(𝐱(t),t,𝐩,y)−(𝐱(1)−𝐱(0))‖2].\mathcal{L}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,\mathbf{x}^{(0)},\mathbf{x}^{(1)},\mathbf{p},y}\left[\|v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(t)},t,\mathbf{p},y)-(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}-\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\|^{2}\right]. (98)

The integrand is G2G^{2}-Lipschitz continuous in θ\theta (by the chain rule and the Lipschitz assumption on vθv_{\theta}) and is bounded:

‖vθ​(𝐱(t),t,𝐩,y)−(𝐱(1)−𝐱(0))‖2≤(2​B)2=4​B2,\|v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(t)},t,\mathbf{p},y)-(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}-\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\|^{2}\leq(2B)^{2}=4B^{2}, (99)

since both 𝐱(1)\mathbf{x}^{(1)} and 𝐱(0)\mathbf{x}^{(0)} are bounded by BB (data) and ‖𝐱(0)‖≤d\|\mathbf{x}^{(0)}\|\leq\sqrt{d} (Gaussian with high probability).

By standard SGD convergence for smooth, bounded losses, after SS steps:

ℒ^TreeFlow ​(θ^S)−ℒ^TreeFlow ​(θ∗)≤O⁡(G2​B2S)=O⁡(1S),\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\hat{\theta}_{S})-\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\theta^{*})\leq O\left(\frac{G^{2}B^{2}}{\sqrt{S}}\right)=O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{S}}\right), (100)

where we absorbed constants.

The hypothesis class for TreeFlow is:

ℱ={(𝐱,t,𝐩,y)↦vθ​(𝐱,t,𝐩,y):θ∈Θ}.\mathcal{F}=\{(\mathbf{x},t,\mathbf{p},y)\mapsto v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},t,\mathbf{p},y):\theta\in\Theta\}. (101)

The key insight is that the path conditioning 𝐩\mathbf{p} partitions the hypothesis class into LL sub-classes, one for each leaf. For a fixed leaf ℓ\ell, the restricted hypothesis class is:

ℱℓ={(𝐱,t)↦vθ​(𝐱,t,𝐩ℓ,y):θ∈Θ}.\mathcal{F}_{\ell}=\{(\mathbf{x},t)\mapsto v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},t,\mathbf{p}_{\ell},y):\theta\in\Theta\}. (102)

The Rademacher complexity of the full class is bounded by the sum over leaves (Mohri et al., 2018):

ℜN​(ℱ)≤∑ℓ=1Lℙ⁡(𝐗∈Rℓ)⋅ℜNℓ​(ℱℓ),\mathfrak{R}_{N}(\mathcal{F})\leq\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{X}\in R_{\ell})\cdot\mathfrak{R}_{N_{\ell}}(\mathcal{F}_{\ell}), (103)

where Nℓ=N⋅ℙ⁡(𝐗∈Rℓ)N_{\ell}=N\cdot\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{X}\in R_{\ell}) is the expected number of samples in leaf ℓ\ell.

For neural networks with WW parameters, ℜN​(ℱℓ)=O⁡(W/Nℓ)\mathfrak{R}_{N}(\mathcal{F}_{\ell})=O(\sqrt{W/N_{\ell}}) under standard assumptions (Bartlett et al., 2017). Under the balanced partitioning assumption, ℙ⁡(𝐗∈Rℓ)≈1/L\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{X}\in R_{\ell})\approx 1/L, so:

ℜN​(ℱ)≤∑ℓ=1L1L⋅O⁡(WN/L)=O⁡(W⋅LN).\mathfrak{R}_{N}(\mathcal{F})\leq\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\frac{1}{L}\cdot O\left(\sqrt{\frac{W}{N/L}}\right)=O\left(\sqrt{\frac{W\cdot L}{N}}\right). (104)

Since the velocity network has O⁡(d)O(d) parameters per dimension (assuming a reasonable architecture), W=O⁡(d⋅D)W=O(d\cdot D) where DD accounts for the depth-dependent embedding. Therefore:

ℜN​(ℱ)=O⁡(d⋅D⋅LN)=O⁡(d⋅L⋅log⁡LN),\mathfrak{R}_{N}(\mathcal{F})=O\left(\sqrt{\frac{d\cdot D\cdot L}{N}}\right)=O\left(\sqrt{\frac{d\cdot L\cdot\log L}{N}}\right), (105)

using D=O⁡(log⁡L)D=O(\log L) for balanced trees.

By standard Rademacher complexity generalization bounds, with NN training samples and batch size BB, after SS steps (so B​SBS total samples seen):

|ℒTreeFlow ​(θ)−ℒ^TreeFlow ​(θ)|≤O⁡(d⋅L⋅log⁡(L/δ)B​S).\left|\mathcal{L}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\theta)-\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\theta)\right|\leq O\left(\sqrt{\frac{d\cdot L\cdot\log(L/\delta)}{BS}}\right). (106)

Combining the optimization and generalization errors:

ℒTreeFlow ​(θ^S)−ℒTreeFlow ​(θ∗)≤O⁡(1S)+O⁡(d⋅L⋅log⁡(L/δ)B​S).\mathcal{L}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\hat{\theta}_{S})-\mathcal{L}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\theta^{*})\leq O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{S}}\right)+O\left(\sqrt{\frac{d\cdot L\cdot\log(L/\delta)}{BS}}\right). (107)

For large LL, the second term dominates (assuming SS and BB are chosen such that B​S≈NBS\approx N), giving:

ℒTreeFlow ​(θ^S)−ℒTreeFlow ​(θ∗)≤O⁡(d⋅L⋅log⁡(L/δ)B​S).\mathcal{L}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\hat{\theta}_{S})-\mathcal{L}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\theta^{*})\leq O\left(\frac{\sqrt{d\cdot L\cdot\log(L/\delta)}}{\sqrt{BS}}\right). (108)

This completes the proof. ∎

Remark H.4 (Sample Complexity vs. Tree Complexity).

The convergence rate’s dependence on L\sqrt{L} reflects a fundamental tradeoff: deeper trees (larger LL) can represent finer-grained partitions and thus more expressive generative models, but require more training data to learn accurately. This is analogous to the bias-variance tradeoff in classical statistics.

Corollary H.5 (Distributional Convergence).

Under Assumption H.2, as S→∞S\to\infty and B​S/N→cBS/N\to c for some constant c>0c>0, the distribution of samples generated by TreeFlow converges in Wasserstein-2 distance to the conditional distributions of the training data within each leaf partition:

limS→∞W2​(pTreeFlow ​(𝐱|𝐩ℓ,y),pdata​(𝐱|𝐗∈Rℓ,y))=0,\lim_{S\to\infty}W_{2}\left(p_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{p}_{\ell},y),p_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{X}\in R_{\ell},y)\right)=0, (109)

where W2W_{2} is the Wasserstein-2 distance.

Proof.

The Wasserstein-2 distance between two distributions with finite second moments can be bounded by the L2 loss of their score functions (Song et al., 2021). Specifically, for two distributions pp and qq on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with scores 𝐬p\mathbf{s}_{p} and 𝐬q\mathbf{s}_{q}:

W22​(p,q)≤C⋅∫0T𝔼𝐱∼pt​[‖𝐬p​(𝐱,t)−𝐬q​(𝐱,t)‖2]​𝑑t,W_{2}^{2}(p,q)\leq C\cdot\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim p_{t}}\left[\|\mathbf{s}_{p}(\mathbf{x},t)-\mathbf{s}_{q}(\mathbf{x},t)\|^{2}\right]dt, (110)

for some constant CC depending on the process parameters.

By Theorem H.10, TreeFlow minimizes the CGTSM objective with path conditioning, which is equivalent to minimizing the integrated score-matching loss. By Theorem H.3, ℒTreeFlow ​(θ^S)→ℒTreeFlow ​(θ∗)\mathcal{L}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\hat{\theta}_{S})\to\mathcal{L}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\theta^{*}) as S→∞S\to\infty.

Since the optimal parameter θ∗\theta^{*} achieves zero loss (by the realizability assumption implicit in our setup), this implies that the learned velocity field converges to the true conditional velocity field:

vθ^S(𝐱,t,𝐩ℓ,y)→v∗(𝐱,t|𝐗∈Rℓ,y)as S→∞.v_{\hat{\theta}_{S}}(\mathbf{x},t,\mathbf{p}_{\ell},y)\to v^{*}(\mathbf{x},t|\mathbf{X}\in R_{\ell},y)\quad\text{as }S\to\infty. (111)

By the connection between velocity fields and score functions (Step 1 of Theorem H.10), this implies score function convergence. By the Wasserstein bound above, this implies distributional convergence in W2W_{2}. ∎

Remark H.6 (Practical Implications).

Corollary H.5 guarantees that with sufficient training, TreeFlow generates synthetic samples whose distribution within each tree partition matches the real data distribution. This is a stronger guarantee than standard generative models provide: TreeFlow not only matches the overall marginal distribution but also preserves the hierarchical structure encoded by the tree.

H.3 Computational Complexity

Proposition H.7 (Training Complexity of TreeFlow).

The computational complexity of training TreeFlow for SS steps with batch size BB using a tree with LL leaves is:

O⁡(S⋅B⋅(L+D⋅Cnet)),O(S\cdot B\cdot(L+D\cdot C_{\text{net}})), (112)

where CnetC_{\text{net}} is the cost of a forward-backward pass through the velocity network and DD is the tree depth.

Proof.

Each training step requires:

  1. 1.

    Sampling BB data points and computing their path encodings: O⁡(B⋅D)O(B\cdot D) (traversing tree to depth DD)

  2. 2.

    Sampling noise 𝐱(0)\mathbf{x}^{(0)} and time tt: O⁡(B⋅d)O(B\cdot d)

  3. 3.

    Computing interpolations 𝐱(t)\mathbf{x}^{(t)}: O⁡(B⋅d)O(B\cdot d)

  4. 4.

    Forward pass through velocity network: O⁡(B⋅Cnet)O(B\cdot C_{\text{net}})

  5. 5.

    Computing loss and gradients: O⁡(B⋅d)O(B\cdot d)

  6. 6.

    Backward pass and parameter update: O⁡(B⋅Cnet)O(B\cdot C_{\text{net}})

The dominant terms are the path encoding (which requires O⁡(D)O(D) traversal per sample) and the network forward-backward passes. For a network with hidden dimension hh, Cnet=O⁡(d⋅h+K⋅h)C_{\text{net}}=O(d\cdot h+K\cdot h) where KK is the path encoding dimension (typically K=LK=L for full decision path representation).

Multiplying by SS steps and simplifying:

O⁡(S⋅B⋅(D+d⋅h+L⋅h))=O⁡(S⋅B⋅(L+D⋅Cnet)),O(S\cdot B\cdot(D+d\cdot h+L\cdot h))=O(S\cdot B\cdot(L+D\cdot C_{\text{net}})), (113)

where we used Cnet=O⁡(d⋅h)C_{\text{net}}=O(d\cdot h) and absorbed the L⋅hL\cdot h term into LL (since typically h=O⁡(d)h=O(d) and L≫dL\gg d for deep trees). ∎

Remark H.8 (Comparison to Standard Diffusion Models).

Standard diffusion models have training complexity O⁡(S⋅B⋅Cnet)O(S\cdot B\cdot C_{\text{net}}). TreeFlow adds an overhead of O⁡(L)O(L) per batch from the path encoding computation. However, this overhead is typically negligible compared to the network cost CnetC_{\text{net}} for reasonably sized trees (e.g., L=256L=256 leaves is small compared to typical network costs). The benefit is that TreeFlow’s path conditioning provides much richer structural inductive bias, often leading to faster convergence and better sample quality.

H.4 Unified View: DSM-Tree and TreeFlow as GTSM Instantiations

We conclude by highlighting the deep structural unity between DSM-Tree and TreeFlow through the CGTSM lens.

Proposition H.9 (Unified CGTSM Framework).

Both DSM-Tree and TreeFlow are solutions to the CGTSM objective under different problem settings:

  1. 1.

    DSM-Tree solves CGTSM for discriminative modeling: learn the coarse-to-fine trajectory of decision boundaries that minimizes classification error.

  2. 2.

    TreeFlow solves CGTSM for generative modeling: learn the coarse-to-fine trajectory of distributions that minimizes generation error (Wasserstein distance).

Both achieve this by explicitly modeling the hierarchical structure encoded in decision trees as a trajectory through tail-equivalence classes (in the discriminative case) or as path-conditioned flow trajectories (in the generative case).

The algorithms differ in their supervision source:

  • •

    DSM-Tree: Supervised by the tree’s discrete decisions d∗​(𝐱,j)∈{0,1}d^{*}(\mathbf{x},j)\in\{0,1\} at each level.

  • •

    TreeFlow: Supervised by conditional flow matching with linear interpolation paths 𝐱(t)=t​𝐱(1)+(1−t)​𝐱(0)\mathbf{x}^{(t)}=t\mathbf{x}^{(1)}+(1-t)\mathbf{x}^{(0)}, conditioned on tree paths.

But both share the same fundamental principle: they discretize the continuous CGTSM trajectory into computationally tractable objectives by leveraging the hierarchical structure of decision trees. This unity demonstrates the power of the CGTSM framework as a universal language for understanding trajectory-based machine learning algorithms.

Theorem H.10 (TreeFlow as Path-Conditioned CGTSM).

The TreeFlow conditional flow matching objective is equivalent to the CGTSM objective with path-specific weighting induced by tree partitions.

Proof.

We establish the connection through three steps: relating flow matching to score matching, incorporating path conditioning, and showing equivalence to CGTSM with structured weighting.

Step 1: Flow Matching as Score Matching.

Conditional Flow Matching (Lipman et al., 2023) trains a velocity field vθ​(𝐱,t)v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},t) by minimizing:

ℒCFM​(θ)=𝔼t,𝐱(0),𝐱(1)​[‖vθ​(𝐱(t),t)−(𝐱(1)−𝐱(0))‖2],\mathcal{L}_{\text{CFM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,\mathbf{x}^{(0)},\mathbf{x}^{(1)}}\left[\|v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(t)},t)-(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}-\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\|^{2}\right], (114)

where 𝐱(t)=t​𝐱(1)+(1−t)​𝐱(0)\mathbf{x}^{(t)}=t\mathbf{x}^{(1)}+(1-t)\mathbf{x}^{(0)} is the linear interpolation.

A fundamental result by Lipman et al. (2023) shows that this objective is equivalent to denoising score matching. Specifically, the conditional velocity field vt​(𝐱(t)|𝐱(1))=𝐱(1)−𝐱(0)v_{t}(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}|\mathbf{x}^{(1)})=\mathbf{x}^{(1)}-\mathbf{x}^{(0)} is related to the conditional score by:

vt​(𝐱(t)|𝐱(1))=σ2​(t)​∇𝐱(t)​log⁡pt​(𝐱(t)|𝐱(1)),v_{t}(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}|\mathbf{x}^{(1)})=\sigma^{2}(t)\nabla_{\mathbf{x}^{(t)}}\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}|\mathbf{x}^{(1)}), (115)

where σ2​(t)=t⁡(1−t)\sigma^{2}(t)=t(1-t) for linear interpolation.

Therefore, minimizing the CFM loss is equivalent to performing denoising score matching with the conditional distribution pt​(𝐱(t)|𝐱(1))p_{t}(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}|\mathbf{x}^{(1)}).

Step 2: Path Conditioning Induces Structured Weighting.

TreeFlow extends the CFM objective by conditioning on both the target sample 𝐱(1)\mathbf{x}^{(1)} and its tree path encoding 𝐩\mathbf{p}:

ℒTreeFlow ​(θ)=𝔼t,𝐱(0),(𝐱(1),𝐩,y)​[‖vθ​(𝐱(t),t,𝐩,y)−(𝐱(1)−𝐱(0))‖2].\mathcal{L}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,\mathbf{x}^{(0)},(\mathbf{x}^{(1)},\mathbf{p},y)}\left[\|v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(t)},t,\mathbf{p},y)-(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}-\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\|^{2}\right]. (116)

The path encoding 𝐩\mathbf{p} identifies which leaf partition RℓR_{\ell} the sample 𝐱(1)\mathbf{x}^{(1)} belongs to. Therefore, we can decompose the expectation by leaf:

ℒTreeFlow ​(θ)=∑ℓ=1Lℙ⁡(𝐗∈Rℓ)⋅𝔼t,𝐱(0),𝐱(1)∈Rℓ​[‖vθ​(𝐱(t),t,𝐩ℓ,y)−(𝐱(1)−𝐱(0))‖2],\mathcal{L}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\theta)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{X}\in R_{\ell})\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t,\mathbf{x}^{(0)},\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\in R_{\ell}}\left[\|v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(t)},t,\mathbf{p}_{\ell},y)-(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}-\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\|^{2}\right], (117)

where 𝐩ℓ\mathbf{p}_{\ell} is the path encoding for leaf RℓR_{\ell}.

This decomposition reveals that TreeFlow implicitly assigns a weight wℓ=ℙ⁡(𝐗∈Rℓ)w_{\ell}=\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{X}\in R_{\ell}) to each leaf partition. This is precisely the structure of a path-dependent weighting in the CGTSM framework.

Step 3: Equivalence to CGTSM with Tree-Induced Weighting.

Recall from Appendix F that the CGTSM objective is:

ℒCGTSM​(θ)=12​∫0Tw⁡(t)⋅𝔼pt∗​(𝐱)​[‖𝐬θ​(𝐱,t)−𝐬t∗​(𝐱)‖2]​𝑑t.\mathcal{L}_{\text{CGTSM}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}w(t)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{x})}\left[\left\|\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},t)-\mathbf{s}_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{x})\right\|^{2}\right]dt. (118)

From Step 1, we know that flow matching is score matching. From Step 2, we see that TreeFlow’s path conditioning induces a decomposition by leaf partitions.

The connection to CGTSM is now clear: the tree structure defines a specific weighting function:

wtree(t,𝐱)=∑ℓ=1L𝕀[𝐱∈Rℓ]⋅ℙ(𝐗∈Rℓ),w_{\text{tree}}(t,\mathbf{x})=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{I}[\mathbf{x}\in R_{\ell}]\cdot\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{X}\in R_{\ell}), (119)

which is a position-dependent and partition-dependent weight.

More precisely, by Theorem C.21, the tree’s hierarchical coarse-graining induces a time-dependent partition sequence {Πtj}\{\Pi_{t_{j}}\} where each partition Πtj\Pi_{t_{j}} at ”time” tj=j/Dt_{j}=j/D corresponds to tree level jj. The CGTSM objective with tree-induced weighting becomes:

ℒCGTSMtree​(θ)=∑j=0D−1∑R∈Πtjℙ⁡(𝐗∈R)⋅𝔼𝐱∈R​[‖𝐬θ​(𝐱,tj)−𝐬tj∗​(𝐱)‖2].\mathcal{L}_{\text{CGTSM}}^{\text{tree}}(\theta)=\sum_{j=0}^{D-1}\sum_{R\in\Pi_{t_{j}}}\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{X}\in R)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\in R}\left[\|\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},t_{j})-\mathbf{s}_{t_{j}}^{*}(\mathbf{x})\|^{2}\right]. (120)

At the finest level (j=D−1j=D-1), this sum over regions R∈ΠtD−1R\in\Pi_{t_{D-1}} is exactly the sum over leaves in TreeFlow’s objective. Therefore:

ℒTreeFlow ​(θ)=ℒCGTSMtree​(θ)|t=tD−1,\mathcal{L}_{\text{{TreeFlow} }}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\text{CGTSM}}^{\text{tree}}(\theta)\Big|_{t=t_{D-1}}, (121)

plus an integration over time t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] for the flow matching formulation.

This establishes that TreeFlow is the CGTSM objective with tree-structured, path-dependent weighting. ∎

Remark H.11 (Comparison to Standard Diffusion Models).

Standard diffusion models use a uniform prior p⁡(𝐱(0))=𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)p(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) and learn a single unconditional score function 𝐬θ​(𝐱,t)\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},t) or 𝐬θ​(𝐱,t|y)\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},t|y) for class conditioning. TreeFlow additionally conditions on the path encoding 𝐩\mathbf{p}, which provides much richer structural information: it encodes the entire hierarchical decision-making process that led to the leaf containing the target sample. This extra conditioning allows TreeFlow to learn separate flow trajectories for different regions of the data space, effectively partitioning the CGTSM objective by tree structure.

Appendix I Experimental Results

This appendix provides detailed descriptions of the experimental setups, model architectures, and training procedures used to generate the results in Section 5. All code was implemented in Python using PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019) for neural networks and Scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) for tree-based models and data processing. All our experiments used a single NVIDIA A100 GPU.

I.1 Details for Verifying the Equivalence (Experiments 1 & 2)

I.1.1 Implicit Tree Structure Discovery (Experiment 1)

Datasets

We use three synthetic 2D datasets generated using sklearn.datasets.make_blobs with 3200 samples each to provide clear, visualizable cluster structures.

  • •

    4_Corners: 4 clusters with centers at (±2,±2)(\pm 2,\pm 2) and a standard deviation of 0.3.

  • •

    9_Grid: 9 clusters in a 3×33\times 3 grid from (−2,−2)(-2,-2) to (2,2)(2,2) with a standard deviation of 0.25.

  • •

    8_Gaussians: 8 clusters arranged in a circle of radius 2 with a standard deviation of 0.15.

All datasets are standardized using StandardScaler.

Diffusion Model

The score network is an MLP implemented in PyTorch. It consists of an input layer mapping the concatenated (𝐱,t)∈ℝ2+1(\mathbf{x},t)\in\mathbb{R}^{2+1} to 128 units, followed by four hidden blocks of (Linear(128) →\to ReLU), and an output Linear(128) →\to 2 layer.

Training

The model is trained for 400 epochs using the Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba, 2015) with a learning rate of 10−310^{-3} and a cosine annealing scheduler. The loss is the standard MSE between the predicted and true noise, as is common in denoising diffusion models (Ho et al., 2020). The forward process uses a linear beta schedule from 10−410^{-4} to 0.020.02 over N=100N=100 steps.

Hierarchy Discovery

The procedure to extract the tree structure is a direct empirical implementation of the theoretical concept from §2.2, performing an agglomerative clustering in the time domain. It discovers the hierarchy encoded by the model’s learned dynamics, not the analytical forward process. The steps are as follows:

  1. 1.

    Initialize Clusters: The process begins with each of the KK ground-truth data classes corresponding to a distinct, active cluster at time t=0t=0.

  2. 2.

    Simulate Learned Forward SDE: For each initial cluster, we simulate its evolution forward in time from t=0t=0 to t=Tt=T. This is not the simple analytical forward process used for training. Instead, we use a discretized Euler-Maruyama scheme to solve the learned forward SDE, where the drift at each step is determined by the model’s own score function: 𝐟learned​(𝐱,t)=[−0.5​βt​𝐱−0.5​βt​𝐬θ​(𝐱,t)]\mathbf{f}_{\text{learned}}(\mathbf{x},t)=[-0.5\beta_{t}\mathbf{x}-0.5\beta_{t}\mathbf{s}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},t)]. This critical step ensures we are analyzing the dynamics the model has actually learned.

  3. 3.

    Track Centroid Trajectories: During the simulation, for each cluster and at each time step tit_{i}, we compute and store two quantities: the geometric centroid of the cluster’s points and their average spread (mean distance from the centroid). This yields a full trajectory for each cluster’s mean and variance over time.

  4. 4.

    Iterative Merge Search: The algorithm proceeds via agglomerative clustering. It iterates until only one cluster remains. In each iteration, it searches for the next merge event by checking every possible pair of currently active clusters to find which pair becomes indistinguishable at the earliest future time.

  5. 5.

    Merge Criterion: Two clusters are defined as ”merged” at the first time step tit_{i} where the Euclidean distance between their centroids becomes smaller than the sum of their spreads. This criterion signifies the moment their probability distributions have substantially overlapped.

  6. 6.

    Dendrogram Construction: The pair of clusters with the minimum merge time is formally merged into a new, larger cluster. The event comprising the two original cluster IDs, the merge time tit_{i}, and the number of original leaves in the new cluster, is recorded. This sequence of recorded merge events directly forms the linkage matrix for the dendrogram, where the vertical axis now represents any discovered merger time tt. The reverse PF-ODE is subsequently used only for visualization purposes.

Additional results for the 9-Grid and 8-Gaussians datasets are shown in Figure 12.

I.1.2 Information Decay Analysis (Experiment 2)

Datasets

We use the MNIST (LeCun et al., 1998), Fashion-MNIST (Xiao et al., 2017), and USPS datasets (Hull, 1994). USPS images are resized to 28×2828\times 28 for consistency.

Tree Entropy Calculation

A DecisionTreeClassifier with max_depth=15 is trained. The resulting model achieves strong performance on the test sets, with classification accuracies of 77.05% on MNIST, 74.15% on Fashion-MNIST, and 85.35% on USPS. These accuracies, being substantially higher than random chance (10%), validate the tree as a high-performing discriminative model. This performance indicates that the tree’s learned hierarchy is not arbitrary; its sequence of splits successfully partitions the feature space in a way that is meaningful for classification. Therefore, we consider the tree’s structure and its corresponding information decay schedule (from low-entropy leaves to high-entropy root) to be a faithful and representative benchmark for the coarse-to-fine organization of the data, against which the diffusion process can be meaningfully compared.

For each depth level, we compute the weighted average of the Shannon entropy (base 2) of the class distributions within each node at that level. This is normalized by the maximum possible entropy, log2⁡(num_classes)\log_{2}(\text{num\_classes}).

Diffusion Entropy Proxy

We use the analytical forward process. The Signal-to-Noise Ratio at time step tt is defined as SNR​(t)=αt/(1−αt)\text{SNR}(t)=\alpha_{t}/(1-\alpha_{t}). Our entropy proxy is defined as 1/(1+SNR​(t))1/(1+\text{SNR}(t)). This function maps SNR ∈[0,∞]\in[0,\infty] to an entropy-like value in [0,1][0,1].

Prototype Visualization

Tree prototypes are the pixel-wise average of all training images passing through a given node. Diffusion prototypes are the states of a single sample after applying the forward diffusion process at various times. Additional results for Fashion-MNIST and USPS are shown in Figure 13.

I.2 Details for Algorithmic Instantiations (Experiments 3 & 4)

I.2.1 DSM-Tree (Experiment 3)

Datasets

We use five publicly available tabular datasets from the UCI repository (Dua and Graff, 2019): Digits (8x8), German Credit, Boston Housing (converted to binary classification), Heart Disease, and Abalone (3-class classification). All features are standardized.

Methodology

The experiment follows three phases:

  1. 1.

    Teacher Model Generation: An oracle RandomForestClassifier (100 estimators, depth 15) is trained. A single DecisionTreeClassifier (depth 15), which serves as our ”Base Tree” baseline, is then trained on the pseudo-labels from this oracle.

  2. 2.

    DSM-Tree Training: A ConditionalSplitModel is trained. This network uses an embedding layer for the tree level jj (embedding dim=32) and a 2-hidden-layer MLP (256 units each, with ReLU and BatchNorm) to predict the split decision. It is trained for 30,000 steps (batch size 256) using Adam with a learning rate of 10−310^{-3}.

  3. 3.

    Inference: To make a prediction, the DSM-Tree model is queried iteratively from level j=0j=0 to simulate traversal down the tree until a leaf is reached.

Results

The detailed performance metrics are provided in Table 2 with a magnified visualization in Figure 14. The results demonstrate that the DSM-Tree model, a fully differentiable neural network, can successfully learn the complex, hierarchical decision logic of a strong tree-based model, achieving comparable and sometimes superior performance.

I.2.2 TreeFlow (Experiment 4)

Datasets

We use a suite of five standard tabular datasets: Adult, Breast Cancer, Diabetes, Wine, and a synthetic California Housing dataset. All are framed as classification tasks and standardized.

Baselines

We compare TreeFlow against four strong baselines: GaussianCopulaSynthesizer, TVAE, and CTGANSynthesizer from the Synthetic Data Vault (sdv) library (Patki et al., 2016), and TabDDPM (Kotelnikov et al., 2023).

Methodology
  1. 1.

    Tree Encoder: A DecisionTreeClassifier (depth 10) is trained. A TreePathEncoder class converts the decision path of any sample into a sparse vector encoding, where the value at an index is the inverse of the node’s depth.

  2. 2.

    TreeFlow Model: The model is a conditional MLP that takes as input (𝐱,t,𝐩,y)(\mathbf{x},t,\mathbf{p},y) and outputs a velocity. It uses embeddings for yy (embedding dim=16) and a 2-hidden-layer MLP (512 units each, with SiLU and LayerNorm). It is trained for 1000 steps using AdamW (l​r=10−3lr=10^{-3}) on the conditional flow matching MSE loss.

  3. 3.

    Generation: We provide a target class label yy and a path encoding 𝐩\mathbf{p} (sampled from a real data point in the desired partition). The model integrates the velocity field via 50 Euler steps from a standard Gaussian noise sample.

Evaluation Metrics
  • •

    TSTR Accuracy (Utility): A RandomForestClassifier (100 estimators) is trained on the synthetic data and evaluated on the real test set.

  • •

    Wasserstein Distance (Fidelity): The average 1-D Wasserstein distance between the marginals of the real and fake test data.

  • •

    Correlation Error (Structure): The Frobenius norm of the difference between the correlation matrices of the real and fake test data.

  • •

    Runtime (Efficiency): Total training time in seconds.

Results

The aggregated mean and standard deviation of all metrics across 5 runs are presented in Table 3. TreeFlow demonstrates a superior trade-off between utility and efficiency, often matching or exceeding the best-performing models in TSTR Accuracy while being more than twice as fast as other diffusion-based methods. A full page visualization is also available in Figure 15.
